notes: A long, flat but sloping call low enough for most people to hear. The three sources that give an average characteristic frequency put it at 11.4 to 12.1 kHz, inside the NSW key's 10 to 15 kHz range; all of these values come from zero-crossing (AnaBat-type) recordings. Pennay et al. warn that harmonics of the Yellow-bellied Sheath-tailed Bat (Saccolaimus flaviventris) fall at 10 to 13 kHz and can be mistaken for this species. What varies: just after take-off and while climbing, Herr and Klomp's bats used shorter, steeper sweeps from up to about 27 kHz down to 13 or 14 kHz, at a faster rate. At a crowded dam in South Australia, Kirkley heard calls with a base of 14 to 15 kHz sweeping down from up to 25 kHz, also faster. Pennay notes that some pulses curve up slightly at the end and that odd pulses in a sequence can jump to about 15 kHz; this is not a regular alternation. No source found a regional difference. The only Victorian data are two bats released at their roost at Mt Big Ben. Start frequency min 11 and max 30 kHz are McKenzie and Muir's range across sequences, so some calls are nearly flat; the above-canopy mean in Victoria was 17.1 kHz. Duration is the least settled number: the Victorian released bats gave 10.4 ms on average, against 16.1 ms (11 to 24 ms) and 12 to 23 ms for free-flying bats in Western Australia, so 14 ms is a middle value. Left out because only one source gives them: end frequency (Herr and Klomp, 11.5 kHz), peak frequency (McKenzie and Muir, 11.5 to 14 kHz in spectral analysis), and call interval (Herr and Klomp, about 430 ms above the canopy, without saying whether this is start to start). The shape's last point, 11.5 kHz, is a drawing choice just below the characteristic frequency, where a QCF call's tail sits.

notes: A loud, low call that many people can hear. It is a shallow downward sweep that levels off near 19 to 20 kHz. Duration: 11.8 ms on average (6.6 to 15.1 ms) in the southern Carnarvon Basin (McKenzie and Muir 2000, 15 sequences, zero-crossing analysis). The Pilbara study gives 8 to 15 ms (20 bats) and the Kimberley study 10 to 17 ms (10 bats), both measured in spectral view. Characteristic frequency: 19.7 kHz (SD 2.1) in the Pilbara, measured as the peak frequency of the main part of the call (FpeakC). The Kimberley mean is 19.2 kHz, Milne (2002) gives 19.8 kHz (95% interval 16.1 to 23.6 kHz) for the Top End, and the Carnarvon mean minimum frequency is 18.6 kHz. Start frequency rests on the Carnarvon study alone (mean 28 kHz, 20 to 40 kHz). The drawn end at 19.2 kHz is a drawing choice just below the typical characteristic frequency. What varies: Milne's Top End reference calls all came from two bats flying together, which gave pulses that alternate in frequency, mixed with steep 'excited' pulses, so Milne calls the sequences messy. That pattern is likely caused by the bats interacting, so the train is drawn as regular. Milne also says Queensland reference calls are sometimes very flat, just below 20 kHz. The Western Australian studies give one call every 1 to 8 wingbeats, so call interval is left out. Similar species: the yellow-bellied sheath-tailed bat (Saccolaimus flaviventris) and Lumsden's free-tailed bat (Ozimops lumsdenae) overlap in frequency. The three Western Australian papers share authors and methods but used different bats in different regions.

notes: Consecutive search calls alternate between a lower and a higher call, and this is the main field mark. Pennay et al. give the low call 28.5 to 30.5 kHz and the high call 30 to 32.5 kHz in southern NSW, the region next to Victoria. Burgess et al. give an Adelaide example pair of 27.5 and 30 kHz. Linke gives an alternating band of 29 to 33 kHz in the SA Murraylands without saying which call is which, so 29 is read as the bottom of the low call and 33 as the top of the high call. The southern NSW figures were used instead of Pennay's all-NSW range of 25 to 34 kHz (the app's current range), because that range includes Doppler-affected calls at the ends of passes. The Western Australian values from McKenzie and colleagues (30.5, 31.5 and 32.5 kHz) pool both calls and fall inside the same band. No Victorian Fc values were found in an opened source. Pennay found no noticeable variation across NSW, and Law (2003) says the call is consistent across the species' range, so values from other states should hold in Victoria. The Victorian AnaScheme key (Gibson and Lumsden) uses a fitted end frequency of 30.61 to 31.30 kHz in one branch, which is a different measure from Fc. The call is curved: a steep start flattening into a tail that sweeps down a little or ends flat, with no harmonics. Calls are steeper in clutter. In open space the high calls can drop out, leaving only low calls (Pennay only). Pennay also says the high call may be shorter and may start no higher than the low call. That detail has one source, so it only guides the drawing: the high shape starts at 47 kHz instead of 50, and both calls share one duration range. Most likely to be confused with the inland broad-nosed bat (Scotorepens balstoni), which Pennay separates by pulse length: under 10 ms against over 10 ms for this species when cruising. Left out for lack of a second source: start frequency (only McKenzie and Muir give one for search calls, about 50 kHz with a range of 39 to 66 kHz, which sets the drawing's start points), end frequency (only the Handbook of the Mammals of the World gives one, 29.6 kHz, from a different recording method; each shape ends just below its call's Fc as a drawing choice), and call interval (only Burgess et al. give one, about 100 to 300 ms and typically 200 to 300 ms, for bats that were probably this species). Peak frequency is left out because the two sources disagree (30.7 to 34.1 kHz against 41.3 kHz) and measured it in different ways. Duration leaves out the handbook's very short calls (printed as 2-7 ms, read as either 2.7 ms or 2 to 7 ms), which look like close-range or hand-release recordings. In montane Victoria and Tasmania some bats end their calls with a pronounced downward droop (Corben and Parnaby 2008); these may be a separate, undescribed species and are not drawn. Xeno-canto has no recordings of this species.

notes: No opened source measured bats in Victoria, so the characteristic frequency (Fc) comes from the regions next to it. The range of 47.5 to 53 kHz covers the two NSW regions that border Victoria in Pennay et al.: 48 to 52 kHz in the Southern region (21 calls) and 47.5 to 53 kHz in the Riverina (9 calls). The South Australian Murray region brochure gives 49 to 52 kHz, inside that range. The typical value of 50.5 kHz is close to the mean (50.3 kHz) of the middle of the Southern NSW range (50), the middle of the Riverina range (50.25), the middle of the SA Murray range (50.5), the Pilbara mean of 50.9 kHz (McKenzie and Bullen, one tagged bat, zero-crossing data) and about 50 kHz in the WA wheatbelt (Bullen and Ford). Sanderson gives about 49 kHz at Belair National Park, SA, for bats that were probably this species. Fc varies by region. Across all of NSW, Pennay et al. give 46.5 to 53 kHz (84 calls). The Tasmanian key (Cawthen) assigns calls of 51.32 to 56 kHz to this species alone and calls of 44.01 to 51.31 kHz to this species or a forest bat (Vespadelus), so Tasmanian bats may call higher than mainland bats. The lower bound of 47.5 kHz sits inside that shared band, and the upper bound of 53 kHz sits inside the band for this species alone. Only that key goes above 53 kHz, so the maximum stays at 53. Call shape: a curved downward sweep that flattens near the Fc and, in search flight, often ends in a short downward tail (Pennay et al.). Cawthen describes the call as L-shaped, sometimes with a slight droop at the end, which could also be read as FM-QCF. McKenzie and Bullen list it as FM to steep FM. The call type stays FM because of the downward tail. The drawing starts at 70 kHz and ends at 48 kHz. Both are drawing choices, because no start or end frequency of search calls is backed by two sources. The flattest part of the drawing sits near 50.5 kHz, the typical Fc, and the last part drops to show the downward tail. Similar species: forest bats that call in the same band. In Victoria these are the little forest bat (Vespadelus vulturnus) and the inland form of the southern forest bat (V. regulus), which calls at 50 kHz or higher along the Murray and can also end in a downward tail. NSW sources also name the eastern forest bat (V. pumilus) and eastern cave bat (V. troughtoni), which overlap with this species at about 49 to 52 kHz. Forest bat calls end with an upturned tail or no tail, while this species often has a downward tail (Pennay et al.; a Sydney consultant report applies the same rule). Pennay et al. say consecutive pulses sometimes alternate a little in shape: every other pulse may start lower, or the bend in the call may step up and down. No source gives two alternating frequencies, so the train is drawn as regular. Pennay et al. also note that hand-released bats of this species take a long time to calm down, and keep giving higher, steeper excited calls before normal search calls. Call length rests on one source so far: McKenzie and Bullen (2009) measured 7 to 8 ms in 63 calls from one tagged bat in the Pilbara, Western Australia. The drawn length, 7.5 ms, is the middle of that range. The Handbook of the Mammals of the World gives about 3.4 ms for south-west Western Australia, with no sample size, so the two sources disagree; check against Victorian recordings when there are some. McKenzie and Bullen give 7 to 8 ms for one bat in the Pilbara, and the Handbook of the Mammals of the World gives 3.4 ms for south-west WA (printed as 3-4, which could also mean 3 to 4 ms). Start, end and peak frequency are left out because only the Handbook gives them: highest frequency 125.8 kHz, lowest 50.4 kHz and peak 63 kHz. These look like close-range full-spectrum measurements, and the 63 kHz peak frequency is a different measure from Fc, so it should not be compared with the Fc range. Call interval is left out because no source gives it in milliseconds; McKenzie and Bullen give one call per one or two wingbeats. Xeno-canto has no recordings of this species.

notes: Calls are curved and often steep, with a long sweep down to the flattest part and no upward hook at the end; now and then the end turns slightly down. All numbers come from AnaBat (zero-crossing) recordings, so no source gives a peak frequency. Characteristic frequency is measured only by Pennay et al. End frequency is measured only by Jolly: minimum frequency 37.4 kHz, plus or minus 1.3. Because the call has no upward hook, its end sits at or just below the characteristic frequency, and the two sources agree, so both are set to a typical 37 kHz. No source gives 34 kHz, the lower bound the app listed before. The Handbook of the Mammals of the World repeats Pennay's 35 to 39 kHz and is not counted as a separate source. Easily confused with the eastern broad-nosed bat (Scotorepens orion) and the greater broad-nosed bat (Scoteanax rueppellii). Calls below 36.5 kHz are hard to separate from S. rueppellii, and Pennay notes overlap with Scotorepens species at 38 to 39 kHz. Pennay says the call does not appear to vary across NSW, that most reference calls were of poor quality, and that the species' range of calls is not well known. Start frequency is left out because only Jolly gives it (mean maximum 50 kHz). Call length and call interval also rest on Jolly alone, from 33 pulses in a south-eastern Australian call library: duration 4.19 ± 1.65 ms and time since the previous pulse 117 ± 7.0 ms (mean ± standard deviation). The file uses the mean as the typical value and one standard deviation either side as min and max. Jolly does not say whether the interval runs from start to start. The shape's first point (50 kHz) uses Jolly's mean maximum frequency as a drawing choice; AnaBat often misses the faint start of a call, so the true start may be higher. Neither source describes alternating calls, so one call is drawn. No Xeno-canto recordings of this species were found under any name tried.

notes: Ghost bats use several kinds of call, and the sketch shows only the brief FM calls that bats gave in flight after leaving a roost. Duration: 4.9 ms on average (SD 0.9, 4 to 8 ms) in the Pilbara (McKenzie and Bullen 2009, Table 4, 10 bats, 44 calls). The Kimberley study (McKenzie and Bullen 2012, 18 bats, 41 calls) gives 3 to 7 ms. Both were measured in spectral view. Frequency: the mean peak frequency of the main part of the call (FpeakC) is 40.5 kHz (SD 5.5, 29.0 to 55.6 kHz) in the Pilbara and 41.3 kHz (SD 5.8) in the Kimberley, so the calls vary widely in frequency. Shape: both studies describe the calls as complex, often W-, M-, N- or U-shaped in frequency over time, or stepped. The sketch draws a plain downward sweep through the typical frequency because no source gives shape points. Its start (55 kHz) and end (32 kHz) are drawing choices inside the measured range. Other calls, not drawn: bats flying back and forth near a mine entrance in the Pilbara gave prolonged calls of 10 to 50 ms, either constant frequency (mean 26.8 ms, 33.6 to 52.6 kHz) or complex FM (mean 22.9 ms); the authors say these may not be search calls. Ghost bats also make audible chirps and twittering sounds. Spacing between calls is usually irregular; where it is regular it follows the slow wingbeat of about 7 per second. No call interval is given. Milne (2002) says calls are so faint and poorly defined on AnaBat that the species would not be identified that way in a general survey. Similar species: the calls share a band with the large-footed myotis (Myotis macropus), long-eared bats (Nyctophilus) and the broad-nosed bats (Scotorepens), and are told apart by their complexity and irregular spacing. The two Western Australian papers share authors and methods but used different bats in different regions.

notes: Older sources call this bat Mormopterus norfolkensis. Search calls are mostly flat, sometimes with a short first section and a short downward tail, and consecutive calls alternate in frequency. All three sources describe the alternation, and Reardon et al. (2008) say no other Australian free-tailed bat is known to alternate. It may call for several pulses without alternating (Pennay et al. 2004). Duration rests on one source: Reardon et al. say search pulses are usually short, 2 to 4 ms, but that the call is very variable. No mean is given, so the app uses the middle of the range. Frequency: Pennay et al. give a characteristic frequency of 31 to 35 kHz (5 NSW calls; 31 to 33.5 kHz in the north east and 32 to 35 kHz in the Sydney Basin). Reardon et al. give 30 to 35 kHz, and the south-east Queensland key (Reinhold et al. 2001, as quoted by Makeham and Conacher 2007) gives minimum frequencies of 30 to 35 kHz. Pennay et al. and Reinhold et al. share three authors, so they count as one source here, with Reardon et al. as the second. The split into a low and a high call comes from Pennay et al.'s Sydney Basin calls (lower pulses 32 to 33 kHz, higher pulses 34 to 35 kHz), and fits Pennay's 'about 2 kHz' and Reardon's '1 to 4 kHz' between the two. The first section, the tail and their depths are drawing choices: no source gives start or end frequency. No source gives call interval. Similar species: Ride's free-tailed bat (Ozimops ridei) calls in the same band but does not alternate and lacks the short first section and downward tail. Gould's wattled bat (Chalinolobus gouldii) also alternates, with a characteristic frequency of 25 to 34 kHz in NSW (Pennay et al.), but its calls are usually curved rather than flat.

notes: No call measurement has two independent sources yet, so this file gives the call type and a rough shape only. Characteristic frequency rests on one source: Bush and Lumsden (2025) give 44 to 50 kHz from unpublished Arthur Rylah Institute reference calls. Conole (1997) gives an average frequency of 48 to 50 kHz, and the Handbook of the Mammals of the World gives a mean frequency of 47.5 to 47.9 kHz and a knee at 48.6 to 49 kHz. Those are different measures from characteristic frequency, and the handbook figures probably come from Conole's work, so they are not counted as a second source. No source found gives call duration, pulse interval, start, end or peak frequency for this subspecies. The shape is a downward sweep that bends into a short tail near 47 to 49 kHz, the band where both the Arthur Rylah Institute figures and Conole's figures sit. The bend comes from the handbook's knee frequency and from characteristic frequency, which by definition marks a flatter part near the end of the call. The shape's start (70 kHz) and end (47 kHz) are placeholders, not measurements. Conole describes this subspecies' calls as steep pulses about 2 to 4 kHz higher than those of the eastern bent-wing bat (M. o. oceanensis, average 43 to 46 kHz). Bush and Lumsden say the two subspecies are hard to tell apart by call and only genetics proves which one it is. The app's earlier range of 43 to 48 kHz is the NSW key's characteristic frequency for the eastern bent-wing bat, not this subspecies. Calls also overlap the little forest bat (Vespadelus vulturnus), southern forest bat (V. regulus) and chocolate wattled bat (Chalinolobus morio), and these are often grouped together as one call type. For the eastern bent-wing bat, the NSW key says call shape and spacing vary within a sequence, while forest bat pulses are evenly spaced; this has not been checked for the southern subspecies. Detection range is thought to be at most 20 to 30 m. Xeno-canto has no Australian bent-wing bat recordings.

notes: Search calls are curved: a steep downward sweep bends into a long, nearly flat section at about 45 to 46 kHz, which often ends in a short downward tail. Call type is FM-QCF rather than plain FM because Pennay et al. (2004), Conole (2000) and Pennay & Lavery (2017) all describe a steep sweep that bends into a long flat section. Similar species: the Large Forest Bat (Vespadelus darlingtoni) and the Southern Forest Bat (V. regulus) call in the same frequency band. Pennay et al. describe the call as often ending in a downward tail, and say that calls with no tail or an upward tail cannot be told apart from V. darlingtoni. They also say that pulse shape and the time between calls usually change within a sequence, so the train is uneven. The Southern Bent-wing Bat (M. orianae bassanii) calls higher: Conole (2000) measured a knee frequency of 48.8 kHz and a mean frequency of 47.7 kHz for it, against 45.8 and 45.4 kHz for this subspecies, and the call frequencies of the two subspecies overlap at the extremes where the two populations meet in central Victoria. Near roost exits and in clutter, calls are steep, almost straight and very variable. Characteristic frequency: the 43 to 48 kHz range comes from Pennay et al. alone (72 NSW reference calls; the 2 calls from southern NSW, the region nearest Victoria, were 44 to 47 kHz). Two other sources put the flat section near the typical value of 45.5 kHz. Conole (2000) gives knee and mean frequency, which are related measures but not characteristic frequency. Pennay & Lavery (2017) give a mean characteristic frequency of 44.1 kHz for Solomon Islands bats tentatively named M. cf. oceanensis, which are not the Australian subspecies. Conole reports that calls are the same from Cairns to Orbost in East Gippsland, but neither his measured sample nor Pennay et al.'s includes a Victorian site. A NSW survey report (Specialised Zoological 2023) separated this species from the two forest bats among calls with a characteristic frequency of 40 to 44 kHz, so some calls may fall below 43 kHz. Left out: start, end and peak frequency, because only the Solomon Islands guide gives them (start about 77 kHz, end 42.4 kHz, peak 47.2 kHz). Call length rests on one source so far, and not one from this subspecies: McKenzie and Bullen (2012) measured 5 to 11 ms in 179 calls from 28 bats in the Kimberley, Western Australia, which are the northern subspecies M. orianae orianae. The drawn length, 8 ms, is the middle of that range. The Solomon Islands guide gives a mean of 4.7 ms for bats only tentatively identified as this subspecies, recorded after capture, which may shorten calls. No source gives a number for the time between calls. Drawing choices: the first shape point (70 kHz) lies inside the Solomon Islands start range of 70 to 80 kHz; the knee at 46 kHz follows Conole; the last point (43.5 kHz) shows the downward tail that Pennay et al. and Specialised Zoological describe, and the depth of that tail is a drawing choice. No Xeno-canto recordings of any Australian Miniopterus were found.

notes: Unlike most molossids, the search call sweeps upward: it starts near 43 kHz and rises to a nearly flat part near 54 kHz. Start, end, duration and interval are the low call of Jung et al. (2014), 77 calls in 11 sequences, given as mean +/- 1 SD. Jung et al. also report a slightly higher upward call (45.5 to 54.8 kHz, 7.6 ms) that alternates with the low one, and occasional downward calls (75.9 to 55.4 kHz, 7.2 ms). Arias-Aguilar et al. found the same two kinds in Brazil: upward type I calls (39.3 to 52.1 kHz, 8.1 ms) and downward type II calls (85 to 52.7 kHz, peak 54.7 kHz). Only the upward call is drawn. Peak frequency is from Arias-Aguilar et al. (type I calls) and is supported by the broadband calls of Guillen-Servent and Ibanez (2007, Venezuela), 45.1 kHz. The end frequency rests on Jung et al. only: the other sources end their upward calls lower, near 50 to 52 kHz (Guillen-Servent and Ibanez 50.4 kHz; the Brazilian highest frequency 52.1 kHz). Calls of bats flying in closed space or after hand release are much shorter, 2 to 4 ms (Oliveira 2015, in Arias-Aguilar et al.). The handbook gives 40 to 50 kHz for the upward search call, probably from Guillen-Servent and Ibanez, so it is not counted as a separate source. Jung et al. recorded in Costa Rica, Panama, Venezuela, Bolivia and Brazil but do not say where each species was recorded.

notes: A steep, almost straight downward FM sweep with no flat tail, made while flying within about 30 cm of the water to catch prey from the surface. Recordings over water can show regular dips in loudness caused by the echo off the water; these are not part of the call. NSW sources call this species the Southern Myotis, and older papers call it Myotis adversus. It is easily confused with the long-eared bats (Nyctophilus). In the NSW key, Myotis calls start with a steeper slope (over 400 octaves per second) and come less than 75 ms apart; calls 75 to 95 ms apart with a starting slope of 300 to 400 octaves per second cannot be separated from Nyctophilus. Start 72 kHz is the mean of three sources: 70 to 80 kHz (NSW), 80.2 kHz (south-east Queensland) and about 62 kHz (Victoria). End 32 kHz is the mean of 35 to 40 kHz (NSW), 31.2 kHz (Queensland) and about 28 kHz (Victoria). The NSW figures come from zero-crossing (AnaBat) recordings, so full-spectrum recordings may show the sweep ending lower. Duration 6 ms is the mean of the three sources and the only value inside both stated ranges: 2 to 6 ms in Victoria (varying with the recording situation), a mean of 5.1 ms in Queensland and 6 to 12 ms in the Kimberley. The maximum of 12 ms comes from the Kimberley only, where calls were measured from frequency-divided recordings. Left out because only one source gives them: peak frequency (35 to 40 kHz, Victoria), characteristic frequency (41.5 kHz, Kimberley) and call interval (the NSW key gives only the under 75 ms identification limit). The Handbook of the Mammals of the World also gives a peak of 80.2 kHz and an interval of 5.1 ms, but these equal its start frequency and call length and look like errors, so they were not used. The NSW key describes a kink near 47 to 50 kHz after which the sweep is less steep; this also rests on one source, so the shape is drawn only slightly curved. Only the Lumsden and Coles abstract is from Victoria, and the NSW reference calls come from the north-east and Sydney, not the south. No Xeno-canto recordings were found.

Duration and call interval come from Mutavhatsindi's free-flying bats at De Hoop (419 calls; mean +/- 1 SD); this is the only free-flight source. Peak is Schoeman and Jacobs' mean +/- 1 SD and has one usable source: the De Hoop value (39.8 kHz) cannot count because the peak was used to pick the calls, and the Zambian peak is higher (46.0 kHz). Free-flying bats at De Hoop called about once every 98 ms; the Zambian release calls came faster (71 ms). Calls are similar to other serotines and house bats near 35 to 40 kHz.

notes: A short, very steep, almost straight downward sweep, like other long-eared bats. Calls are quiet. Duration: 5.6 ms on average (SD 1.0, 3 to 7 ms) in Pilbara mangroves (McKenzie and Bullen 2009, Table 4, 6 bats, 65 calls, partly from Bullen and McKenzie 2002). The Kimberley study (McKenzie and Bullen 2012, 11 bats, 136 calls, recorded in the Kimberley) gives 4 to 10 ms. Both were measured in spectral view. Frequency: the Pilbara mean peak frequency of the call (FpeakC) is 51.3 kHz (SD 2.1, 48.2 to 57.6 kHz) and the Kimberley mean is 52.0 kHz (SD 2.7). In a steep call like this the value is close to the middle of the sweep. Milne (2002) gives a characteristic frequency of 47.1 kHz (95% interval 40.1 to 54.1 kHz, 8 Top End calls). The Handbook of the Mammals of the World gives 50 to 52 kHz without a source. No source gives start or end frequency. The drawn start (72 kHz) and end (47 kHz) are drawing choices that keep the sweep inside the app's 35 to 75 kHz range and end near Milne's characteristic frequency. Sequences can include occasional calls outside the species' normal frequency range, which the authors call departure sub-sequences (Pilbara 48 down to 38 kHz, Kimberley 48 to 44 kHz); these are not drawn. Call interval is left out: the studies give one call per wingbeat but no time. Similar species: Milne says its calls cannot be told from other long-eared bats (N. geoffroyi, N. bifax and N. walkeri) on AnaBat, and the Kimberley study could not separate it from N. daedalus. The ghost bat (Macroderma gigas) and the large-footed myotis (Myotis macropus) use the same band. The two Western Australian papers share authors and methods but used different bats in different regions.

notes: This call is very hard to tell from the calls of other long-eared bats. Pennay et al. (2004) say it overlaps almost completely with Gould's long-eared bat (N. gouldi), and also with N. bifax and N. timoriensis. The large-footed myotis (Myotis macropus) is the other common confusion. Pennay et al. separate the two species by the slope at the start of the call (usually under 300 octaves per second in this species, over 400 in the myotis) and by the pulse interval, which is usually over 95 ms in this species. The bat calls softly, so recordings often show only short fragments of each call, and the start frequency depends on how close the bat is to the microphone. Calls from western NSW are lower and longer than calls from eastern NSW. Social calls recorded in the Riverina are longer than 10 ms and sweep from 45 to 50 kHz down to 20 to 25 kHz; this sketch shows only the search call. All the numbers come from zero-crossing (AnaBat) analysis, so full-spectrum recordings may show a wider sweep and longer calls. Start frequency: the range 65 to 80 kHz is from Pennay et al. and McKenzie and Muir (2000); the mean in Jolly's south-eastern call library is lower, 62 kHz. End frequency is from Pennay et al. (35 to 47 kHz) and Jolly (mean 41 kHz). Characteristic frequency comes only from Western Australian studies (means of 42.5 kHz in the Carnarvon Basin, 47.3 kHz in the Pilbara and 47.4 kHz in the Kimberley); no south-eastern source gives one. The typical value of 45 kHz is the midpoint of the Carnarvon and Pilbara means. Duration: 4 ms is the average of three means (Jolly 2.7 ms, McKenzie and Muir 4.3 ms, Pilbara 5.4 ms). Kimberley bats measured on a spectrogram had calls of 4 to 12 ms; those values are left out of the range. Pulse interval: 90 ms is between Jolly's measured mean of 87 ms and the 95 ms that Pennay et al. give as the usual lower limit. Only Jolly measured the interval, so the file gives no interval range. Peak frequency is left out because only one study measured it (McKenzie and Muir: 40.1 to 49.4 kHz in 22 Western Australian calls). The 47 to 48 kHz peak frequency in the Handbook of the Mammals of the World repeats an earlier Western Australian zero-crossing value that is closer to a characteristic frequency. The shape is a steep, almost straight sweep that flattens slightly near 45 kHz and then drops more steeply to the end, as Pennay et al. describe. Xeno-canto has no recordings of any Nyctophilus species (checked November 2026).

notes: The call is a steep, almost vertical FM sweep. Both the NSW call guide (Pennay et al. 2004) and the Handbook of the Mammals of the World say so, and both say it cannot be told apart from other long-eared bats on typical recordings. The NSW guide names the lesser long-eared bat (Nyctophilus geoffroyi), N. bifax and the species it calls N. timoriensis, and says the calls overlap almost completely on standard AnaBat measurements. It separates this species from the large-footed myotis (Myotis macropus) by a pulse interval usually over 95 ms and an initial slope under 300 octaves per second; Myotis is under 75 ms and over 400 octaves per second, and values in between are ambiguous. That 95 ms figure is the guide's threshold for telling the two apart, not a measured interval. Calls are quiet and often appear as short fragments. The bat finds prey mostly by listening for prey sounds and gleans it from foliage or the ground, using echolocation mainly to find its way, so call trains may be sparse or missing in cluttered habitat. The start, end and peak frequencies that follow are left out of the fields. Start frequency is 65 to 80 kHz and end frequency usually 35 to 43 kHz (NSW guide, 56 reference calls). The start is where the visible zero-crossing trace begins, so it depends on how close the bat was, and full-spectrum recordings may start higher. The guide found little difference between NSW regions. In the Riverina, the NSW region next to Victoria, calls average 68 kHz at the start and 42 kHz at the end (16 calls). The Southern NSW row (67 to 45 kHz) is identical to the same row in the N. geoffroyi account, so it may be a copy error and is not used. Peak frequency is 50 to 53 kHz, mean 51.8 kHz (Handbook of the Mammals of the World, which gives no region or sample size). For call interval there is only the NSW threshold given earlier. Herr et al. (1997) give a mean time between pulses of 142 ms, but its standard deviation (162 ms) is larger than the mean, which suggests gaps from missed pulses were counted, so it is not used. Call length rests on one source: Herr et al. (1997) measured 2.8 ms on average (SD 0.9 ms) from 54 pulses of 13 bats on the western slopes of the Australian Alps near Albury. The range given is the mean plus or minus one SD. Their bats were recorded with AnaBat as they flew off after being released by hand, and such calls can be shorter and steeper than in normal search flight. Figures for N. geoffroyi were not borrowed. The app's current range of 35 to 80 kHz is the NSW guide's lowest end frequency and highest start frequency joined into one span. The Batica page from Bayside, Melbourne repeats it under a 'Characteristic Frequency Range' heading, but it is the whole sweep, not the characteristic frequency, and that page copies the NSW guide's identification notes word for word, so it is not a second source. Herr et al. (1997) give AnaBat means of 62.3 kHz maximum, 39.8 kHz minimum and 46 kHz characteristic frequency (SD 5.9) for this species, but these have not yet been reconciled with the NSW guide, so they are not used as fields. The drawn call starts at 68 kHz and ends at 42 kHz, the Riverina averages, which are single-source values used only to place the line. Its slope eases slightly toward the end. No source mentions alternation, so the regular train is the default for a single call type, not an observation. Xeno-canto has no recordings of any Nyctophilus species.

notes: Check the taxonomy before using this entry. Since Parnaby's 2009 revision, Nyctophilus major is the long-eared bat of south-western Western Australia and southern WA and SA east to the Eyre Peninsula. It is not known from Victoria. The bat once called the greater long-eared bat in Victoria (the south-eastern form of N. timoriensis) is now N. corbeni, which the Victoria list already has as its own entry, so this entry may count one bat twice. The app lists it as Greater long-eared bat; the Handbook of the Mammals of the World calls N. major the Western long-eared bat. The call is a very steep, near-vertical FM sweep. The handbook and the NSW call guide both say long-eared bats (Nyctophilus) cannot easily be told apart by call. Calls are soft, so sequences are often fragmentary. The handbook says it hunts mostly from a perch, finding prey by listening with its large ears, and probably uses echolocation in some cases. No number has two independent sources, so every number is left out. Peak frequency rests on one source: the handbook gives 42 to 47 kHz (mean 44.4 kHz) for WA animals, probably taken from Bullen and McKenzie (2001), which could not be read. No source gave start or end frequency, characteristic frequency, duration or call interval for N. major. The shape's start (70 kHz) and end (40 kHz) are drawing choices, not measurements: a steep, almost straight sweep that passes through the handbook's peak range. For comparison only, the NSW call guide measured the eastern bat now called N. corbeni (a different species) at about 70 to 71 kHz falling to 42 to 43 kHz on average, with an AnaBat mean frequency of 53 kHz. The same guide separates long-eared bats from Myotis by a call interval over 95 ms and a gentler initial slope (under 300 octaves per second); that rule is for the genus and was not measured for this species. notes: Older sources call this bat Mormopterus beccarii. The Handbook of the Mammals of the World says Australian bats once placed in M. beccarii are this species, ranging from the Pilbara east across northern Australia, so the Pilbara and Kimberley 'M. beccarii' data are used here. The call is a shallow, curved downward sweep. Duration: 6 to 14 ms in the Kimberley (McKenzie and Bullen 2012, 6 bats, 118 calls) and 8 to 13 ms in the Pilbara (McKenzie and Bullen 2009, 6 bats, 85 calls), both measured in spectral view. Neither gives a mean, so the app uses the middle of the range. The southern Carnarvon Basin study (McKenzie and Muir 2000) gives 10.1 ms (6.1 to 13.2 ms) for 'M. beccarii', but the Carnarvon Basin lies south of the range given in the handbook, so that study is not counted. Characteristic frequency: 26.3 kHz (SD 1.6) in the Pilbara, measured as the peak frequency of the main part of the call (FpeakC); 27.6 kHz (SD 1.3) in the Kimberley. Milne (2002) gives 24.3 kHz (95% interval 20.3 to 28.4 kHz), but from 5 Queensland reference calls, because none had been collected in the Top End. The handbook gives a peak frequency of about 24 kHz. No source gives start or end frequency for this species' range. The drawn start (31 kHz) and end (26 kHz) are drawing choices; the start is near the Carnarvon mean maximum frequency of 32.2 kHz. Call interval is left out: the Western Australian studies give one call every 1 to 4 wingbeats. Similar species: Milne says it overlaps the yellow-bellied sheath-tailed bat (Saccolaimus flaviventris) and needs a discriminant function to separate them, and it just overlaps Gould's wattled bat (Chalinolobus gouldii) at 28.2 to 28.4 kHz. The two Western Australian papers share authors and methods but used different bats in different regions.

notes: Older call keys name this species Mormopterus species 4 (long penis form), and the NSW call guide (Pennay et al. 2004) uses that name. Search calls are flat or slightly curved pulses, sometimes ending in a short downward sweep. Consecutive calls keep the same frequency and shape: they do not alternate. Characteristic frequency (Fc) in the NSW reference calls is 26 to 30.5 kHz (30 calls), and 26.5 to 30.5 kHz in the Riverina, the NSW region next to Victoria. Sanderson (1995) gives about 27 kHz for bats recorded in Belair National Park, South Australia, which he identified from their calls only. The typical Fc of 27.5 kHz is close to the mean of Sanderson's 27 kHz and the middle of the NSW range (28.25 kHz). The maximum of 30.5 kHz comes from the NSW guide only. No Victorian Fc values were found in a source that could be opened. In a 2017 online discussion, G. Ford and T. Reardon say flat pulses can go as low as 24 or 25 kHz, but this is opinion rather than measurement, and Reardon says it of the inland free-tailed bat (Ozimops petersi) as well, so the minimum stays at the NSW guide's 26 kHz. Similar species: Gould's wattled bat (Chalinolobus gouldii) calls in the same band, but its calls alternate in frequency or shape and never show a harmonic. Calls between 30 and 30.5 kHz cannot be told apart from the inland free-tailed bat. Upper-harmonic pulses of the yellow-bellied sheath-tailed bat (Saccolaimus flaviventris) can also be confused with this species. An automated key built from northern Victorian reference calls (Gibson & Lumsden 2003) separates this species from Gould's wattled bat in one branch by the lower curvature of its pulses. The NSW guide reports a harmonic of the same shape at about 53 to 60 kHz in some calls, and odd pulses near 40 kHz in the Riverina. The harmonic is not drawn because only the NSW guide reports it and the guide gives no strength for it. Two cautions about the NSW guide: a 2022 consultant report passes on G. Ford's view that the guide's Ozimops reference calls are believed to contain errors, and the guide's text says it has no reference calls from the Southern region while its figure page shows a Southern sequence at about 27 to 30 kHz. Left out because no opened source gives them for this species: call duration, call interval, start frequency, end frequency and peak frequency. Without a call duration the sketch cannot be drawn to scale. Western Australian values for 'Mormopterus planiceps' (McKenzie & Muir 2000; Bullen 2003) are not used, because those bats are now placed in other Ozimops species. The drawn call starts at 31 kHz, an assumed value, drops quickly, and then stays nearly flat to the typical Fc. Ending the drawing at the typical Fc is a drawing choice, because no source gives an end frequency. Xeno-canto has no recordings of this species.

notes: Older call keys and papers call this species Mormopterus species 2 or the eastern free-tailed bat. The search call is a flat pulse (QCF on AnaBat recordings) that does not alternate in frequency from one pulse to the next, although the NSW guide says the odd pulse in a sequence can be higher. Characteristic frequency is 28.5 to 31 kHz in the NSW guide (Pennay et al. 2004), from only two reference calls, both from north-east NSW. A key for south-east Queensland and north-east NSW (Reinhold et al. 2001, quoted by Makeham & Conacher 2007) gives 29 to 36 kHz but does not say which frequency it measured. It may be minimum frequency, which in a flat call with no tail is close to the characteristic frequency. The typical 30 kHz is the middle of the 29 to 31 kHz band where the two ranges overlap. The minimum of 28.5 kHz rests on the NSW guide alone, and the maximum of 36 kHz rests on the Reinhold key alone. A consultant report from the Sydney area passes on a remark by G. Ford that the NSW guide's reference calls for this genus may contain errors, so the NSW range is weak. That report treats a call as flat when its initial slope is under 100 octaves per second. An automated key built from reference calls in northern Victoria (Gibson & Lumsden 2003) assigns pulses that end at 30.6 to 31.3 kHz, with low curvature and an almost level start, to this species. That is one step of the key, not the species' full range, but it fits the drawn shape. The same study identified all its reference calls of 'Mormopterus sp. eastern', probably this species, though the article does not say so. Similar species: the east coast free-tailed bat (Micronomus norfolkensis) calls in the same band, but its calls alternate in frequency and have a short first section and a downward sweep at the end, which this species lacks. Gould's wattled bat (Chalinolobus gouldii) also calls near 30 kHz but alternates its frequency. In the Victorian key, pulses ending near 31 kHz can also come from Gould's wattled bat or from the free-tailed bat the key calls Mormopterus lp (probably the southern free-tailed bat, Ozimops planiceps), and the key separates this species by its low curvature and level start. notes: A long constant-frequency call with a short upward sweep at the start and a short downward sweep at the end. Constant frequency: the NSW guide gives a characteristic frequency of 66 to 70 kHz across NSW (36 calls) and 66.5 to 70 kHz in Southern NSW (15 calls), the region next to Victoria. Fullard et al. (2008) measured a mean peak frequency of 68.6 kHz in south-east Queensland, and Robson et al. (2012) give about 68 kHz in Papua New Guinea. The typical 68 kHz is the midpoint of the NSW range. The maximum was 74 kHz before; that came from Coles (2002), a conference abstract that gives 67 to 74 kHz in passing, with no data, place or method. No other source goes above 71 kHz (the Handbook of the Mammals of the World, for north-east Queensland), so the maximum is now the NSW guide's 70 kHz. Call length and interval come from one study only: Fullard et al. (2008) recorded bats flying inside two disused mines in south-east Queensland and one near Cairns, not in open search flight. They measured a mean call length of 52.9 ms and a mean gap of 55.4 ms from the end of one call to the start of the next, so calls start about 105 ms apart (52.9 + 55.4 = 108 ms; from their mean duty cycle of 51.7%, 102 ms). End frequency: Fullard et al. give the terminal sweep as 12.2 kHz below the constant frequency, ending near 56 kHz; Robson et al. give a drop of about 8 kHz (to about 60 kHz) from AnaBat recordings, which tend to lose the faint end of a sweep. No source gives the start frequency of the upward sweep or how long either sweep lasts, so the first shape point (64 kHz) and the times of the second and third points are illustrative. Victorian bats belong to the nominate subspecies, found in eastern NSW and eastern Victoria. The Handbook says Queensland populations seem closer to Rhinolophus achilles than to Victorian bats, so Queensland values may not apply in Victoria. The NSW guide says no other NSW species has a call like this one, and that harmonics with the same shape sometimes show; no source gives their level, so none are drawn. No source reports alternation, so the train is drawn as regular. Xeno-canto has no recordings of this species.

notes: A short constant-frequency call that begins and ends with a brief frequency sweep, as in other leaf-nosed bats. Bats from the Kimberley and the Top End call lower: the Kimberley mean is 116.5 kHz (SD 2.8), and Milne (2002) gives 116 kHz (95% interval 107 to 125 kHz, 6 calls). The Handbook of the Mammals of the World also reports this difference (mean 114.6 kHz in northern Australia and 121 kHz in the Pilbara) but does not say where its numbers come from. The Pilbara values are used because that study measured the most bats; Kimberley and Top End bats will sit near the bottom of the drawn range. Weak calls in the Pilbara sometimes read 55 to 110 kHz, which the authors treat as recording artefacts. The depth of the sweeps at the start and end is a drawing choice: no source measures it. notes: No call measurements from Victoria were found, where the species is a rare summer visitor. The numbers come from New South Wales and Western Australia, plus one reference call of unknown origin that was supplied with the ANABAT system. The search call is long and narrowband: it drops a few kHz and levels off. It is usually slightly curved but can be flat. Flat calls tend to be longer, and curved calls higher and shorter. Many people can hear it. Characteristic frequency is usually 18 to 19 kHz. The NSW guide gives 17.5 to 22.5 kHz, with most calls in an 18 to 20 kHz band, and Western Australian sequences go down to 15 kHz. A sequence sometimes switches to another harmonic for a pulse or two, most often at 28 to 33 kHz, where it can be mistaken for Gould's wattled bat. Odd single pulses can fall anywhere from 15 to 24 kHz. The White-striped Free-tailed Bat is also audible but calls lower, around 11 kHz. In northern Australia the Bare-rumped Sheathtail Bat calls slightly higher and is hard to tell apart, but it does not occur in Victoria. Sources disagree on which harmonic the 18 to 20 kHz band is: the NSW guide treats it as the main harmonic with less common pulses at 9 to 13 kHz, while the Pilbara study puts the fundamental near 16 kHz. Detectors show the 18 to 20 kHz band, so only that band is drawn and no harmonics are listed. Start frequency comes from two zero-crossing measurements of the highest detected frequency (means of 20.8 and 24.1 kHz); full-spectrum recordings may show a higher start. Peak frequency rests on two studies that share a lead author: known bats from the Carnarvon Basin, and Kimberley sequences that were identified with a rule that already required 14 to 21 kHz and pulses longer than 17 ms. The Kimberley values are that paper's averaged peak frequency measured on full-spectrum recordings, not a zero-crossing figure. End frequency is left out because only the ANABAT reference call gives it (18.8 kHz, the same as its characteristic frequency, so that call ends at its flattest part). The shape's last point (18.5 kHz) is set to the typical characteristic frequency. Call interval is left out: the ANABAT reference call gives 221 ms between pulses from a single sequence, and the Western Australian studies say one call is made every 1 to 10 wingbeats, so spacing is irregular and often several hundred ms. Xeno-canto has no recordings of this species.

notes: Characteristic frequency differs by region. In NSW it is 28 to 34 kHz, and 29 to 34 kHz in the Riverina, the NSW region next to Victoria, so Victorian calls are most likely in that range. In the southern Carnarvon Basin, Western Australia, it averages 34.3 kHz (range 32.5 to 36.5 kHz), about 4 kHz higher than in NSW, and the Handbook of the Mammals of the World notes that S. balstoni may be more than one species. The typical value of 33 kHz is inside both regional ranges. In open areas the bat may switch to sloped cruise calls at about 28 kHz. The call is a curved FM sweep that flattens near its end. The tail varies: usually it sweeps down or is missing, and sometimes it sweeps up. Similar species: Gould's wattled bat (Chalinolobus gouldii) generally calls at lower frequencies and alternates its call frequency. Both species give cruise calls at 28 to 29 kHz, and above 30 kHz only Gould's wattled bat alternates. The free-tailed bat that the NSW guide calls Mormopterus species 3 has flat calls with an initial slope under 100 octaves per second (OPS), while S. balstoni calls are curved with an initial slope usually over 200 OPS. The greater broad-nosed bat (Scoteanax rueppellii) has its knee above 37 kHz and a pre-characteristic drop of more than 3 kHz. In the Western Australian study, S. balstoni calls overlapped little broad-nosed bat (Scotorepens greyii) calls. Duration: the Western Australian study measured a mean of 4.2 ms (range 3.5 to 4.9 ms) for search and approach calls, and the NSW guide gives cruise calls as usually 7 ms and always under 10 ms. The typical 5.5 ms is the midpoint of those two values, and each flight phase has only one source. Left out because only one source gives them: peak frequency, 34.1 to 38.7 kHz (7 calls, Western Australia); start frequency, mean 65.8 kHz and range 57 to 74 kHz (Western Australia); and the knee, the bend between the steep sweep and the flat tail, which the NSW guide puts below 37 kHz and usually at 31 to 33 kHz. The Handbook of the Mammals of the World and Wikipedia list the Western Australian peak frequency range as characteristic frequency. No source gives call interval or end frequency. The drawn call starts at 60 kHz, inside the Western Australian start range but below its mean because NSW calls are lower, and ends at the typical characteristic frequency. The regular call train rests on the NSW guide alone: the guide separates Gould's wattled bat from this species by alternation, which implies that S. balstoni does not alternate. Start frequency rests on the Carnarvon study alone: 24.9 kHz on average, 24.0 to 26.5 kHz, so the call drops only about 1 kHz. The drawn end (24.0 kHz) is close to the Carnarvon minimum frequency and is a drawing choice. The three studies come from two research groups: the two Western Australian papers share authors and methods but used different bats in different regions. Call interval is left out. The Western Australian studies give one call every 1 to 7 wingbeats, so spacing varies. Similar species: Hill's sheath-tailed bat (T. hilli) could not be told apart in the Pilbara, and the Arnhem sheath-tailed bat (T. kapalgensis) in the Top End uses much shorter calls (under 8 ms). Beccari's or Lumsden's free-tailed bat (Ozimops lumsdenae) overlaps in frequency but its calls are curved. The Handbook of the Mammals of the World gives a peak of 25 kHz without a source.

notes: A curved FM sweep that flattens into its lowest, flattest part near the end of the call, and usually ends with a short upward sweep. The Handbook of the Mammals of the World calls the call FM/QCF. Calls in a sequence keep the same frequency, with no alternation. The flat part is drawn at 45 kHz because both frequency sources put it there: the NSW guide gives a characteristic frequency of 44.5 to 45.5 kHz for the only calls confirmed by a museum specimen (2 calls from the Riverina, the NSW region next to Victoria), and Bullen and McKenzie (2019) give a peak frequency of typically 44 to 47 kHz. These are different measures with one source each, so neither is given as a number in this file. The NSW guide's wider range of 39 to 46 kHz (23 calls) comes mostly from 21 calls recorded at Nanya in far western NSW, which may be from the little forest bat (V. vulturnus) or from both species. The guide also lists the Riverina among regions with no reference calls, which contradicts its own Riverina figure, and labels its example Riverina call with a question mark. Bullen and McKenzie do not say where their calls were recorded. No source gives start or end frequency, call duration or call interval, so these are left out. The drawn start of 60 kHz, and the end of 46.5 kHz that shows the upward sweep, are drawing choices, not measurements. Similar species: the little forest bat overlaps in frequency (47 to 48 kHz in the north west of NSW, 43 to 50 kHz in the Riverina), and the NSW guide says this species is hard to identify in the field. The little pied bat (Chalinolobus picatus) calls at similar frequencies but alternates its call frequency. When looking for the bristle-faced free-tailed bat (Setirostris eleryi), Bullen and McKenzie left out sequences with every call above 43 kHz, because those overlap this species in frequency and call shape. The regular call train and the upward tail rest on the NSW guide alone. Xeno-canto has no recordings of this species or of any other Vespadelus.

notes: This sketch uses values from southern NSW and the NSW Riverina, next to Victoria, and from the South Australian Murraylands. The characteristic frequency changes gradually across the range: in NSW it falls from the north-east to the south-east and rises again further west (Pennay et al.). Pennay et al. give 40 to 44 kHz for most of southern NSW, 38 to 40 kHz in the far south-east corner next to East Gippsland, and 40 to 44 kHz in the Riverina (5 calls), with a shift to higher frequencies towards the west. The sample size printed after the south-east corner figure (17 calls) may refer to the whole southern region. Linke gives 40 to 42 kHz in the South Australian Murraylands without naming the measure. The minimum of 38 kHz rests on Pennay's south-east corner figure alone. The maximum of 44 kHz is the top of the southern NSW and Riverina ranges. The typical value of 42 kHz is the middle of those ranges, the top of Linke's range, and close to the mean minimum frequency (41.9 kHz) and fitted curve minimum (42.1 kHz) that Jolly measured. Over all of NSW the range is 38 to 46 kHz (89 calls), the range the bat book gives, and it reaches 43 to 48 kHz near the Queensland border. The Handbook of the Mammals of the World gives 38 to 48 kHz, which repeats the NSW data. Gibson and Lumsden say the range is much wider in northern Victoria than further south, filling the gap between 40 and 50 kHz, but they give no figure, so calls above 44 kHz from northern Victoria may still be this species. Their northern Victorian key could name the species for fewer than 40% of its reference calls; the rest went to species groups or unknowns. Call shape: a curved downward sweep that flattens into a flat section near the characteristic frequency. Pennay et al. say the flat section is often long and the tail is absent or turns up, with some down-turned tails in the Riverina. The Handbook calls it a broad FM/QCF call. So the call type is FM-QCF rather than the plain FM the app listed, and the drawing bends early and has a long flat tail. The drawing starts at 54 kHz, the mean maximum frequency from Jolly, the only source for start frequency. That figure comes from zero-crossing recordings, so the start seen on full-spectrum recordings is probably higher. The drawing ends flat at 42 kHz, the typical characteristic frequency, because no second source gives an end frequency. Pennay et al. say pulses in a sequence are even and consecutive, so the train is drawn as regular; this rests on that one source. Similar species: the southern forest bat (Vespadelus regulus) calls in the same band in southern NSW and Victoria. In southern NSW its flat section is usually shorter than 1.8 ms, but the large forest bat can also have a short flat section (Pennay et al.). Lentini et al. pooled the two species as one 40 to 45 kHz group in the NSW wheat-sheep belt, and Linke gives the southern forest bat as about 42 kHz in the same survey without saying how the two were separated. In Jolly's table the large forest bat has a lower minimum frequency (41.9 kHz) than the southern forest bat (44.2 kHz) and the little forest bat, Vespadelus vulturnus (45.0 kHz). Bent-wing bats (Miniopterus) call in a similar range, but their pulse shape and spacing change within a sequence, while large forest bat pulses are even and consecutive and lack a downward tail (Pennay et al.). Start and end frequency are left out because only one source gives them. Call length and call interval rest on that one source (Jolly) until a second is found; the file uses the mean as the typical value and one standard deviation either side as min and max. Jolly measured 433 pulses pooled from whole files in the South-eastern Australian bat call library at Charles Sturt University: duration 4.76 ± 1.63 ms, time since the previous pulse 97 ± 13 ms, maximum frequency 53.8 ± 8.0 kHz and minimum frequency 41.9 ± 1.8 kHz (mean ± standard deviation). A review in the same newsletter issue notes that some of the large forest bat files may have needed calibrating. No source gives peak frequency. The Pennay et al. and Jolly figures come from zero-crossing (AnaBat) recordings, and Linke names neither the measure nor the recording mode, so none is given as peak frequency. Xeno-canto has no recordings of this species or genus.

notes: This sketch shows the southern form of the call, which is the form heard across southern and eastern Victoria. Bats in northern Victoria call about 10 kHz higher. Along the Murray River west of Albury, the characteristic frequency is 50 to 55 kHz in the NSW Riverina (Pennay et al., 38 calls) and 51 to 57 kHz in northern Victoria (Gibson and Lumsden). Riverina calls often end in a long downward tail and rarely go below 50 kHz. Lentini et al. and the Handbook of the Mammals of the World give 54 to 55 kHz for this high form, but both repeat the NSW data of Law et al. (2002), and the Handbook labels it southern NSW. Pennay et al. report an abrupt change near Albury: bats at Albury, Hume Dam and further west call at 50 kHz or higher, while bats at Tabletop (30 km north of Albury) and Tumbarumba call at 40 to 44 kHz. A call near 52 kHz from the Murray plains can still be this species. Together the two forms cover 39 to 57 kHz. Characteristic frequency of the southern form: 40 to 44.5 kHz in southern NSW (Pennay et al., 29 calls); 39 to 47 kHz in southern Victoria (Gibson and Lumsden, quoting Duffy et al. 2000, with the measure not named); 41.6 to 44 kHz in Tasmania (Cawthen, in a key step that does not separate this species from the large forest bat); and about 42 kHz in two South Australian surveys (Linke, and Sanderson, whose identification was tentative). The minimum and maximum cover the southern NSW and southern Victoria ranges. The typical value of 42 kHz is the middle of the southern NSW range and matches the South Australian figures. The Handbook gives 40 to 43 kHz for south-eastern NSW, which repeats the NSW data. Call shape: a steep downward sweep that bends into a short flat section near the characteristic frequency. Pennay et al. describe the call as curved, Cawthen as L-shaped, and the Handbook as steep FM/QCF, so the call type is FM-QCF. In southern NSW the flat section is usually shorter than 1.8 ms (Pennay et al.), so the drawing bends late and has a short tail. The tail varies and can turn up or down. The drawing ends flat at 42 kHz, the typical characteristic frequency, because no second source gives an end frequency. The drawing starts at 60 kHz, close to the mean maximum frequency of 60.7 kHz measured by Jolly, which is the only source for start frequency. Similar species: the large forest bat (Vespadelus darlingtoni) calls in the same band, and the Tasmanian key (Cawthen) and the NSW farmland key used by Lentini et al. group the two species together. Pennay et al. say this species usually has a shorter flat section, but large forest bat calls can be short too. Jolly found almost no difference between the calls of this species and the little forest bat (Vespadelus vulturnus): a discriminant analysis in that study classed 77% of southern forest bat pulses correctly. Bent-wing bats (Miniopterus) call in a similar range, but their pulse shape and spacing change within a sequence, while southern forest bat pulses are even and consistent (Pennay et al.). In the Riverina the high form overlaps the chocolate wattled bat (Chalinolobus morio), which tends to alternate its pulse shape. Start and end frequency are left out because only one source gives them. Call length and call interval rest on that one source (Jolly) until a second is found; the file uses the mean as the typical value and one standard deviation either side as min and max. Jolly measured 162 pulses from the South-eastern Australian bat call library at Charles Sturt University, with the recording locality not stated: duration 3.84 ± 1.07 ms, time since the previous pulse 87 ± 7.3 ms, maximum frequency 60.7 ± 8.6 kHz and minimum frequency 44.2 ± 1.4 kHz (mean ± standard deviation). The regular call train rests on Pennay et al. alone. No source gives peak frequency from full-spectrum recordings. All frequencies here are characteristic, minimum or maximum frequencies measured from zero-crossing (AnaBat) recordings, so none is given as peak frequency. Xeno-canto has no recordings of this species.

notes: Characteristic frequency (Fc) differs between regions, sometimes abruptly. The Fc range in this file covers Victoria and the NSW regions next to it. Pennay et al. give 44 to 47 kHz for southern NSW (from Eden west across the Great Dividing Range to the South West Slopes, next to eastern and north-eastern Victoria) and 44.5 to 51 kHz for the Riverina (next to northern Victoria). Kutt's AnaBat II readings of bats released in East Gippsland, Victoria, are 44.5 and 46 kHz in free flight. These are cursor readings, not formal Fc measurements. Jolly measured a mean minimum frequency of 45 kHz in a south-eastern Australian call library, which matches a flat part near 45 to 46 kHz. The typical Fc of 46 kHz is inside both NSW ranges and equal to the higher of Kutt's two free-flight readings (44.5 and 46 kHz). The upper limit of the app's current range (45 to 53 kHz) matches the values for coastal NSW north of Narooma (49 to 53.5 kHz) and the Sydney Basin (48.5 to 53 kHz), and neither region is in Victoria. Across all of NSW, Fc is 42.5 to 53 kHz. A Landcare survey in the South Australian Murraylands gives 48 to 55 kHz and does not say which frequency it measured. Gibson and Lumsden report that in northern Victoria, where the southern forest bat (Vespadelus regulus) calls at 51 to 57 kHz, the calls of little forest bats and large forest bats cover a wider frequency range, including the 40 to 50 kHz band. They give no figures, so calls from northern Victoria may fall outside this file's range. The Handbook of the Mammals of the World describes three distinct call types across the species' range and says they may belong to separate species. Call shape: a curved FM sweep that flattens near its end, almost always followed by a prominent upward-sweeping tail (Pennay et al.). The tail is the main field mark, but no source gives its height, so the drawing ends at the typical Fc without a tail. Calls are flatter in open areas. Fc can drift by up to 4 to 5 kHz within one sequence, which Pennay et al. put down to Doppler shift as the bat circles. Above the canopy, Kutt recorded paired pulses (a short steep pulse, then a longer shallow pulse) about 153 ms apart; the drawing does not show these. Similar species: on AnaBat measurements, southern forest bat calls are nearly identical to little forest bat calls (Jolly), and two of Jolly's little forest bat files came from females that may have been southern forest bats. Away from the coast, calls below 44 kHz can overlap with the large forest bat (Vespadelus darlingtoni) (Pennay et al.). Bent-winged bats (Miniopterus) give uneven consecutive pulses, while little forest bat pulses are even in shape and spacing. Duration: Jolly's mean over 362 pulses is 3.45 ms (standard deviation 1.28 ms). Kutt's readings for a bat on a harness (3.18 ms) and in a small room (4.92 ms) fall on either side of that mean, so the typical duration is 3.5 ms and the minimum (2.2 ms) is Jolly's mean minus one standard deviation, rounded. Kutt's two free-flight readings, 7.67 and 9.56 ms, are much longer than Jolly's mean. Each is one pulse picked with the AnaBat cursor, so the maximum of 9.6 ms comes from a single pulse. Interval: Jolly's mean is 90 ms (standard deviation 14.5 ms), and Kutt's free-flight and harness readings are 89.5 and 86.6 ms. The minimum and maximum are Jolly's mean minus and plus one standard deviation. Neither source says whether its interval runs from the start of one call to the start of the next. Jolly divided gaps of two or three times the median gap to allow for missed pulses, and dropped longer gaps. Kutt's 51.1 ms interval (bat in a small room) and 153 ms interval (paired pulses above the canopy) are left out because neither is search flight. The regular call train is based on Pennay et al. alone: they describe consecutive pulses as even, and no source discusses alternation. Left out: start frequency, because only Jolly gives one (mean 63 kHz, file means 58.4 to 67.5 kHz); the drawing starts at 63 kHz. End frequency, because only Jolly gives a related value: a minimum frequency of about 45 kHz, which for a call with an upward tail is the bottom of the curve, not its end. Gonsalves et al. (2013) give an end frequency of 50 to 53 kHz, but for coastal NSW bats, and Law, a co-author of Pennay et al., is one of its authors. Peak frequency, because no source gives it; Fc is a different measure and is not used in its place. The drawn curve averages about 50 kHz, close to Jolly's mean frequency of 50.1 kHz. The call type is FM because Pennay et al. and Kutt both describe a curved FM call; the Handbook of the Mammals of the World calls it FM/QCF. Xeno-canto has no recordings of this species.
